AI Quick Read Anshuman Rath and Babar Hayat produced stunning performances with the bat as Hong Kong stunned Sri Lanka by just one run to finish seventh at the Hong Kong Sixes 2026 on Sunday. Having finished second in their respective groups during the round-robin stage, both Hong Kong and Sri Lanka advanced to Plate Cup semifinals. However, losses in Plate Cup semifinals pitted both teams together for a 7th-8th place playoff match. In the semis, Hong Kong lost to Pakistan while Oman downed Sri Lanka. Sent into bat first, Hong Kong started in a blistering note with Hayat and Rath going bonkers from the first over. Also Read | BAN vs IND, Hong Kong Sixes 2026: India secure first win to finish 11th After just two boundaries in the first over by Lankan Sangeeth Cooray, both the Hong Kong openers upped the ante in the second and there was no looking back. They were particularly brutal in the third over bowled by Chamindu Wijesinghe, smashing three sixes and two fours in a 29-run over. Rath brought up his fifty in just 17 balls with a six over deep mid-wicket off Movin Subasingha in the fourth over, before retiring hurt according to tournament rules. While the fifth over only yeilded seven runs for Hong Kong, it was two sixes each from Nizakat Khan and Hayat in the final over that propelled them to 119/0 in six overs. How did Sri Lanka reply in chase? While Rath finished at 51, Hayat remained unbeaten on 44 (16b), Nizakat took 14 runs from his four balls he faced. In reply, Vishen Halambage started on a fiery note for Sri Lanka with 14 runs in the first four balls of the chase before being caught by Hayat in the fifth delivery off Nasrulla Rana. Also Read | England vs India: Rahul Tripathi's 14-ball 56 goes in vain at Hong Kong Sixes More success awaited Hong Kong in the second over as Yasim Murtaza struck twice to dismiss Sachitha Jayatilake and Subasingha to derail Sri Lanka. Muditha Lakshan 58 not out and Cooray (24, 8b) did try their best but in the end Sri Lanka fell short by just one run. Who is Anshuman Rath? All you need to know Anshuman's roots belong to Satyanagar in Bhubaneswar, Odisha. After his father Tarang left India for business, Rath was born in Hong Kong in 1977. Anshuman started playing cricket at the age of four and attended the West Island School in Hong Kong. During his age-group cricket days, Anshuman played for Hong Kong U-16 and also represented Middlesex for their U16 and U17 teams. He finally made his Hong Kong debut in 2014 in ODIs and in T20Is a year later. In fact, Anshuman also captained Hong Kong in international cricket. However, Anshuman retired from the Hong Kong national team in 2019 to pursue a career in India. Two years later, he became eligible to play for Odisha in 2021-22 domestic season as an Indian passport holder. But lack of opportunities in India forced him back to Hong Kong. Also Read | IND vs UAE: India stumble to second consecutive loss at Hong Kong Sixes 2026 He returned to the Hong Kong squad for the Quadrangular Series in March 2023. In franchise cricket, Anshuman played for Edmonton Royals in the 2019 Global T20 Canada. About the Author Koushik Paul Koushik lives and breathes sports. A 2017 Journalism and Mass Communication graduate from Maharaja Manindra Chandra College, Kolkata, Koushik has reported on high-profile events including the FIFA U17 World Cup 2017, Ranji Trophy, FIH Pro League, FIH World League finals, the Indian Premier League, and Lionel Messi’s historic visit to Kolkata in 2025.

While he possesses a versatile command over all sports, he finds his niche in cricket, specializing in breaking news, long-form interviews, global sporting updates, and high-energy live blogs. Koushik’s professional perspective was further sharpened through the 2020 AIPS Young Reporters Programme, where he gained invaluable insights from renowned international journalists, including Keir Radnedge and Riccardo Romani from the United Kingdom, and Martin Mazur from Argentina. Currently based between Kolkata and Delhi, Koushik remains at the forefront of the breaking developments that shape the public sporting discourse. When he isn't tracking scores or deconstructing plays, he can be found exploring new landscapes on his travels or channeling his creative energy into the kitchen.
